claims.claim: Merwin tells writers to ask which encounter elements are better shown on a map than described in prose.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Outlines and Frameworks', D&D Beyond, 9 Oct 2019
claims.quote: better represented in a map rather than strictly described in the text

claims.claim: For sandbox adventures Merwin recommends a less detailed encounter description leaning on the NPCs' resources so the DM can set it in any of several places.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Thinking Like a Designer', D&D Beyond, 2020
claims.quote: a less-detailed description that relies on place

claims.claim: Merwin makes the test of an adventure's layout whether it serves the DM running it at the table.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Thinking Like a Designer', D&D Beyond, 2020
claims.quote: serves the DM who will be running your content

claims.claim: Hartlage reports that Gygax's own Castle Greyhawk key gave most rooms a one-line note.
claims.quote: he usually wrote a 1-line note for each room

claims.claim: Judges Guild's Bob Bledsaw said referees told him they wanted only a skeletal framework of description.
claims.source: Bob Bledsaw, Dragon #27, quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2016

claims.claim: Hartlage credits Gygax's longer location descriptions in G1 Steading of the Hill Giant Chief (1978) with setting the pattern for later adventures.
claims.quote: set the pattern for virtually every adventure to follow

claims.claim: Hartlage identifies the padding mechanism: the convention of long descriptions makes authors stretch a good middle sentence to an assigned length.
claims.quote: pads it like a school paper stretched to an assigned length

claims.claim: Hartlage argues a location's length of description should follow its purpose in play, so a sheriff's kitchen needs no inventory.
claims.quote: no one needs an item-by-item inventory of her kitchen
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage warns that excess description buries the details that would actually enter play.
claims.quote: An avalanche of description does more than squander page count
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage's defence of boxed text is that it consolidates and marks which features need describing.
claims.quote: consolidates and identifies features that require description

claims.claim: Hartlage observes that Storm King's Thunder (2016) omits almost all read-aloud text, unlike Curse of Strahd which boxes every location.
Michael Curtis describes the one-page-dungeon style of Stonehell as giving the minimum information needed to run the dungeon.
claims.source: Michael Curtis, quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: the minimum amount of information needed to run the dungeon

claims.claim: Hartlage's rule for a dungeon key is that descriptions carry telling details and plot-critical information.
claims.quote: focus on telling details and plot-critical information

claims.claim: B11 King's Festival (1989) told DMs that good description goes beyond sight to noises, smells and touch.
claims.source: Carl Sargent, B11 King's Festival (TSR, 1989), quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2024
claims.quote: A good DM details more than simply what PCs see
claims.page: B11 King's Festival (1989) — Description and the senses

claims.claim: Keep on the Shadowfell (2008) told DMs to distinguish NPCs with an accent or favourite saying, a signature object, or a single personality adjective.
claims.source: Bruce Cordell and Mike Mearls, H1 Keep on the Shadowfell (2008), paraphrased with a quoted adjective list by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2024
